It's legal to make a deal if you play through each turn of "discard, go!
discard, go! discard, go!" until the conditions of withdrawal are met.
But then again, it's also perfectly legal for a player to break that deal
in the meanwhile and attempt to oust his prey (or at least stop the
withdrawal from succeeding).

Messages.Author: Gregory Stuart Pettigrew
Messages.Body:



It may seem kind of strange that you can't "mutually concede", but you all
need to *actually* withdraw before time runs out.

The fastest method for this is to slap a card out of your hand, say
"Done", and replace while the next player is taking his turn. If you start
your turn with less than a full hand, then say "I Withdraw - Done". If you
get to your next turn with no funny business, go buy yourself a soda while
everyone else tries to get to where you were - and hopes you don't
accidentally win the tournament for getting your 1 VP while they all
timeout and get .5.

Be sure to take into account all mandatory effects, but try to avoid any
optional effects. Also, be sure to stack your hand with defensive cards
(especially the 0-cost bounces and Obedience/Bloodstorm of Chorazin) in
case your predator decides to break the deal.

--
- Gregory Stuart Pettigrew

Messages.Author: quickbeam
Messages.Body:
Robert Goudie wrote:

>
> Good or bad, time limits are a necessity for running tournaments.
>
> -Robert

I've heard some horror stories of tournaments going until dawn, so I
understand this argument in its broad strokes. However, I still think
it is worth thinking about and discussing the effects that time limits
have on the game, because it isn't a value neutral proposition. As an
aside, as long as changing fonts and layouts is so common, the design
team could stop calling it the Eternal Struggle, and start calling it
the Two Hour Struggle.

Now, I don't feel that time limits unduly impair my enjoyment of the
game, I just find them irksome, and worth discussing. Many times I've
been told of the problems created by games that go on too long, often
with regards to the outside world, and players having demands on their
time besides VTES, which is fine. If I am not mistaken, though, the
upcoming prerelease in Boston (which I am excited about and plan on
attending - thanks for running it, Josh) is going to be three
preliminary rounds followed by a final, each of which has a two hour
time limit. I think 8 hours of VTES destroys any outside world
arguments (at least for one day), and I'm interested in why it is three
2 hour prelims instead of two 3 hour prelims.

In the larger scheme of things, it isn't a huge deal. I don't think it
is "bad for the game." Obviously, the core player base and design team
embrace this state of affairs and it works well enough, but it has an
impact. The option of table timeouts is extremely distasteful to me
personally, as it skews overall victory to decks that show early
promise but lack staying power. I am more interested in the
discussion (if others believe it is worth their time to discuss) of how
time limits and time outs affect metagame and deck choice.

-Dave Clooney, wishing everything could be just a tad more eternal.

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
quickbeam wrote:
> I've heard some horror stories of tournaments going until dawn, so I
> understand this argument in its broad strokes. However, I still think
> it is worth thinking about and discussing the effects that time limits
> have on the game, because it isn't a value neutral proposition.

The effect that time limits has is that it makes people do stuff. This
being said, I am rarely in tournament games that go to time, and in
tournaments that I judge, the vast majority of games finish before time
is up. Yeah, occasionally, a game times out due to an extreme parity,
but mostly they end in a timely manner. So in reality, what time limits
do is force people to play the game in a timely manner as opposed to
dicking around for 4 hours. As *most* games, likely, get finished in 2
hours or less, it seems reasonable to expect that games get done in 2
hours.

This being said, I'm perfectly in favor of adding an extra half hour on
to the final rounds of big tournaments, if for no other reason than to
see if it helps games end, as big tournaments tend to time out a lot.
But it is arguable that adding time to the game wouldn't really help,
as finals tend to time out as one of the players has all the incentive
in the world to make it time out (if no one is ousted, 1st seed wins in
a time out...)

> Now, I don't feel that time limits unduly impair my enjoyment of the
> game, I just find them irksome, and worth discussing. Many times I've
> been told of the problems created by games that go on too long, often
> with regards to the outside world, and players having demands on their
> time besides VTES, which is fine. If I am not mistaken, though, the
> upcoming prerelease in Boston (which I am excited about and plan on
> attending - thanks for running it, Josh) is going to be three
> preliminary rounds followed by a final, each of which has a two hour
> time limit. I think 8 hours of VTES destroys any outside world
> arguments (at least for one day), and I'm interested in why it is three
> 2 hour prelims instead of two 3 hour prelims.

'Cause most games end in 2 hours or less anyway. And three hour games
tend to really only benefit a small number of players (the people
winning) and hurt a larger number of people (the people ousted early
who have to sit around for an extra hour doing nothing). And three
games gives more room for error and more room for more people to do
well than two games. And I suspect, in reality, that most folks don't
want to play a single game of VTES for that long.

> In the larger scheme of things, it isn't a huge deal. I don't think it
> is "bad for the game." Obviously, the core player base and design team
> embrace this state of affairs and it works well enough, but it has an
> impact. The option of table timeouts is extremely distasteful to me
> personally, as it skews overall victory to decks that show early
> promise but lack staying power. I am more interested in the
> discussion (if others believe it is worth their time to discuss) of how
> time limits and time outs affect metagame and deck choice.

I honestly don't think that it makes *that* much of a difference in
terms of deck choice--I mean, yeah, ok, knowing a game has to end in 2
hours might disuade you from playing a really slow wall deck, but
again, as it is likely that most games end in 2 hours or less anyway,
what you have is people playing decks with forward momentum. Which I'd
argue is good for the game in any case.

-Peter

Messages.Author: quickbeam

My principle concern is that "in a timely manner" manifests most often
through extensive use of dominate.

>As *most* games, likely, get finished in 2
> hours or less, it seems reasonable to expect that games get done in 2
> hours.

I agree with your premise but draw the opposite conclusion. Most of
the time, no matter what the limit is, the game will finish in under
two hours. I think it is worth extending the time limit beyond two
hours because time outs are awful.

>
> This being said, I'm perfectly in favor of adding an extra half hour on
> to the final rounds of big tournaments, if for no other reason than to
> see if it helps games end, as big tournaments tend to time out a lot.

I am very much with you on this one. The one place where a timeout is
supremely unsatisfying is in the final. It stands to reason that
timeouts that aren't the result of slowplay (through either ineptitude
or stalling) are often the result of a balanced table; a final table is
often a balanced table of the best decks, by design of the tournament.
No one who didn't make the final needs to sit in the stands and watch
it to the end (thanks in large part to the TWD archive and fun to read
tournament reports).

Someone always has an incentive to time the final table out, and maybe
just a half hour or an hour (to a total of three) added on would be
enough that no one could deliberately time out the table without
visibly stalling.

> 'Cause most games end in 2 hours or less anyway. And three hour games
> tend to really only benefit a small number of players (the people
> winning) and hurt a larger number of people (the people ousted early
> who have to sit around for an extra hour doing nothing).

They don't have to sit there doing nothing. They can play pick up
games and converse about VTES. Tournaments favor people who are
winning. The early ousts can play in the loser's bracket with a spare
deck. I'll run and get coffee if I'm there (I'm sure I'll be in the
loser's bracket plenty of times).

>And three
> games gives more room for error and more room for more people to do
> well than two games.

I am not in favor of leaving more room for error. Tournaments should
punish error. I want each game I play in to really matter, and I don't
want the sneak bleed deck with an early oust in a game that went to
time to get a higher seed. Yes, this is a partisan attack on sneak
bleed, and a partisan defense of wall decks .

>And I suspect, in reality, that most folks don't
> want to play a single game of VTES for that long.
>

That is fine too. As long as there is a bit of thoughtful debate, I'm
satisfied whether or not people agree.

>
> I honestly don't think that it makes *that* much of a difference in
> terms of deck choice--I mean, yeah, ok, knowing a game has to end in 2
> hours might disuade you from playing a really slow wall deck, but
> again, as it is likely that most games end in 2 hours or less anyway,
> what you have is people playing decks with forward momentum. Which I'd
> argue is good for the game in any case.
>
> -Peter

I disagree that "forward momentum" is good for the game in any case. I
think playing quickly and focusing on winning the table are good for
the game, but they aren't the same thing as forward momentum.

Turbo Arika will still win games under a three hour time limit, as will
weenie dom et al. Having a few more minutes might allow an alternative
to riding the table into the ground for folks trying other strategies.
I'm arguing that a lot of heavy pool damage dealing capability at the
expense of other things can turn the game into a race, instead of a
multiplayer game, and I think this is bad.

I also think it is possible that the group that plays this game, on
the whole, has improved, and that correspondingly tournament play has
improved. If there is a nut at a table that is just walling up for no
good reason, and shows no signs of working forward, I'm confidant that
the rest of the players will crack that nut.

I at least want to see if a three hour final makes the sky fall. I've
had it said to me more than once that two hours is a minimum, but it
appears that the minimum is the maximum in most actual tournaments.

Anyway, thanks for the response.

-Dave Clooney

However, there is an element of luck involved in the shuffle (unless
you're one of the cheaters, that is). Enough iterations of a deck's

provide an accurate indicator of a deck's true performance.

> I disagree that "forward momentum" is good for the game in any case. I
> think playing quickly and focusing on winning the table are good for
> the game, but they aren't the same thing as forward momentum.

What do you think "forward momentum" is, then? Because what you just
described is an excellent definition of "forward momentum" -- along with
offense being stronger than defense, people attempting to oust their
prey, etc. etc.

> I'm arguing that a lot of heavy pool damage dealing capability at the
> expense of other things can turn the game into a race, instead of a
> multiplayer game, and I think this is bad.

Everyone agrees that having NOTHING but 100% pool-damage decks is bad
for the game. But having forward momentum doesn't mean playing nothing
but weenie Dominate.

> improved. If there is a nut at a table that is just walling up for no
> good reason, and shows no signs of working forward, I'm confidant that

I'm not, because past history has shown enough timeouts to make me not
confident. Especially when the player walling up has enough cross-table
influence to deal out damage to anyone interfering with him.

> I at least want to see if a three hour final makes the sky fall. I've
> had it said to me more than once that two hours is a minimum, but it
> appears that the minimum is the maximum in most actual tournaments.

I think that any step towards longer games is a step further away from
gaining new players.

Derek

>

I'm more than happy with the standard two hour limit for a number of
reasons. Firstly I would start to lose enjoyment once the clock ticked
past the two hour mark, the game would become an endurance test.
Secondly I have no problem with timeouts. I don't see why people find
them unsatisfying. I actually enjoy timeouts. I prefer a table where
there is real struggle compared to a table where one deck dominates (no
pun intended).

Time limits certainly affect how I design my decks. I have a deck at
the moment that is very slow which I know I have to modify if I intend
bringing it to a tournament. Some of my decks are designed to time the
game out after i've gained two vps. One of my favourite cards is
Millicent Smith which is fantastic for slowing down a game.

We play two hour time limit in our social games to so that our decks
are suited to a tournament environment (as well as to make sure we get
enough games in of an evening).

You say that timeouts skew victory to decks that lack staying power but
that depends on how you define staying power. If you accept the two
hour time limit then staying power becomes a deck that can last two
hours.

Chris.

> I agree with your premise but draw the opposite conclusion. Most of

> hours because time outs are awful.

Sure. But as most games end under 2 hours, it is reasonable to expect

awful, is necessary to keep games from going on forever which holds up
the whole tournament.

> They don't have to sit there doing nothing. They can play pick up

> winning. The early ousts can play in the loser's bracket with a spare
> deck. I'll run and get coffee if I'm there (I'm sure I'll be in the

Sure. But an extra hour of sitting around and getting coffee is a

I mean, like, this is likely the result of wildly divergent world view,

them time out) than 2 games.

> I am not in favor of leaving more room for error. Tournaments should

> want the sneak bleed deck with an early oust in a game that went to

A) Extra room for error means that the wall deck that gets ousted in 4
minutes due to sitting down next to the dominate weenie deck and had
critical deck error isn't totally hosed.

B) Wall decks can't win games regardless of the time limits--2 VPs in a
5 player game isn't likely to win.

> I disagree that "forward momentum" is good for the game in any case. I
> think playing quickly and focusing on winning the table are good for
> the game, but they aren't the same thing as forward momentum.

???

Forward momentum means you can go forward. Going forward makes the game
work. Again, this is likely the result of wildly divergent world view
that is unlikely to be resolved, but personally, I don't think wall
decks (i.e. decks that exist solely to defend themselves and maybe oust
folks obtusely via Smiling Jack or something) are good for the game
much at all as they slow things down and tend to throw the game towards
their predator. Like, sure, I don't want ever deck in the game to be a
weenie dominate deck, but I vastly prefer to play games where all the
decks can, ya know, oust their prey through proactive measure. And if
extending the time limit meant that more folks were encouraged to play
slow, ponderous wall decks, I'd vote No on Proposition Extend Time
Limits in a second.

> Turbo Arika will still win games under a three hour time limit, as will
> weenie dom et al. Having a few more minutes might allow an alternative
> to riding the table into the ground for folks trying other strategies.

I don't think an extedned time limit will help. 'Cause turbo Arika and
weenie dominate will still win in 20 minutes, and slow wall decks still
will only get 2VPs in a 5 player game. Only with a longer time limit,
the people who get run over by Turbo Arika and weenie dominate have a
lot longer to sit around before they get to play again.

> I'm arguing that a lot of heavy pool damage dealing capability at the
> expense of other things can turn the game into a race, instead of a
> multiplayer game, and I think this is bad.

Sure. But extending the time limit isn't going to change this--with a 3
hour game, fast dominate heavy decks *still* will be, ahem, dominant.
And the slow, ponderous wall decks *still* aren't going to win that
much. This is a factor of the structure of the game, not the time
limits.

-Peter

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <1131459774.5...@g14g2000cwa.googlegroups.com>,

pd...@lightlink.com writes:
>I mean, like, this is likely the result of wildly divergent world view,
>but given 6 hours, I would *much* rather play 3 games (even if some of
>them time out) than 2 games.

It's probably also worth noting that while the example tournament
brought up was three two-hour rounds, then a final, many tournaments can
happily run as two two-hour rounds, then a final.

If you start reasonably early in the morning, that can give you most of
the afternoon to go off and do other things if you don't get into the
final. Or it can mean you run a tournament from mid afternoon into the
evening. 8 hour tournaments block off a lot of time, which means that
some people will be less likely to play in them.

I'd be loathe to alter the flexibility that tournament organisers have
now to run shorter tournaments which don't eat up people's entire day
off, whilst still having the capacity to run five round, two day, super-
sized tournaments when they want to.

Messages.Author: CthuluKitty
Messages.Body:
>I appreciate the posts. I'll quiet down about the time limit and just
>encourage folks to move through their turns a little quicker.

I think is one of the most important things that causes the time limit
to be a problem in some instances. Ideally, a time limit should
uniformly encourage players to play faster, but the way the time limit
is implemented in VTES it does not. In fact, it often gives players a
very good reason to play slower, which is technically cheating but
nearly impossible to rule on. In chess, time control is not a problem
because each player has a seperate clock that only ticks when it's your
turn. Obviously this would be nearly impossible to implement in a
multi-player, action/reaction based game like VTES. However, it would
be interesting to establish some kind of rubric for deciding how long
is too long in making certain kinds of decisions. For example, how
long is it acceptable to tolerate a player staring at their hand
deciding whether or not to block an action, or which vampire to hunt
with first, or repeatedly varifying that they are still holding 7 cards
despite not having done anything? At the moment, such decisions are
entirely up to a judge's discretion, with no guidelines suggested by
the VEKN rules, and it's my general impression that slow play is almost
never penalized unless a player is flagrantly stalling. Other
considerations here are players engaging in excessive table talk
(whether relevant or external to the game) and/or not paying attention
to what's going on when it's not their turn. These things have a high
potential of slowing the game down, which often ends up penalizing
other players instead of those actually responsible for the delay.
